new.definition: Raw fish or shellfish, sliced or served whole, and dressed at the last moment with little more than olive oil, salt and citrus. The word is Italian for raw, and on a menu it is short for pesce crudo, raw fish. The seafood is never cooked, by heat or by a long soak in acid, so its own sweetness and texture lead. Because it is raw, a crudo carries the consumer advisory the house uses for raw food.
new.guest: Crudo is the Italian word for raw: the seafood comes to you raw, dressed just before it leaves the kitchen with citrus and a little seasoning. Ours is sweet bay scallops with Meyer lemon, black truffle and crisp radish, cool and bright, a light way to begin.
new.kitchen: The seafood is held cold and dressed to order, never ahead, so the acid has no time to firm it. Every raw dish goes out with the house's raw food advisory, and the cut and the portion are the kitchen's to say at lineup.
new.compare: Ceviche is its nearest neighbor: in ceviche the fish sits in a good deal of citrus until its surface turns firm and opaque, while a crudo is dressed lightly at the last moment and keeps the texture of raw fish.

new.background: Crudo is Italian for raw, and pesce crudo, raw fish, belongs to the coasts of Italy. Sicily has long eaten raw fish, and Bari, on the Adriatic in Puglia, keeps a tradition of crudo di mare, a plate of raw octopus, cuttlefish, mussels, clams and sea urchin. As a word on American menus, crudo is newer: it reached a wide public after an Italian seafood restaurant opened in New York in 2000 with raw fish at the heart of its menu, and in 2007 NPR called it Italian sashimi. The American dish is usually thin slices of raw fish or shellfish dressed with olive oil, salt and citrus, sometimes a little vinegar, just before it goes out. On Thanksgiving Day the Brennan's menu used the word for its raw bay scallops.

new.definition: A lemon hybrid from China, rounder than a common lemon, with a thin, smooth skin that ripens deep yellow with an orange tint. Its juice is sweeter and less acidic than that of the Eureka and Lisbon lemons sold in most stores, and its peel is fragrant. The trees grown in the United States today are the Improved Meyer, a virus free selection released in 1975.
new.guest: A Meyer lemon is a sweeter, gentler lemon, thin skinned and deep yellow, brought to America from China in 1908. It brightens the raw scallops without the sharp sourness of a common lemon, so their sweetness comes through.
new.kitchen: Its juice and zest are milder than a common lemon's, so a dressing is tasted before more is added. Whether the crudo carries juice, zest or segments is a lineup question.
new.compare: The common Eureka or Lisbon lemon is sharper and more acidic, with a paler, thicker peel; the Meyer is sweeter, thin skinned and a deeper yellow, near orange when ripe.

new.background: The Meyer lemon carries the name of Frank N. Meyer (1875 to 1918), a plant explorer for the United States Department of Agriculture who collected across China and Central Asia and sent home more than 2,500 introductions. In 1908 he brought this lemon from near Peking, today Beijing, and it was entered as plant introduction 23028. In the 1940s it was found to carry the tristeza virus without showing it, a danger to other citrus, so its planting was banned in some citrus areas and many trees were pulled out. In 1967 a University of California text judged it acceptable as a lemon for home use but not satisfactory as a commercial variety for the fresh fruit trade. A virus free selection found at a California nursery in the 1950s was certified and released by the University of California in 1975 as the Improved Meyer lemon, the tree sold ever since.

new.definition: The crisp, juicy root of Raphanus sativus, a member of the mustard family, eaten raw for its crunch and its peppery bite. The small red globe is the familiar kind; others grow long and white, as daikon does. The heat is not in the whole root: it forms when the radish is cut or chewed, and it fades as grated radish stands.
new.guest: The radish adds crunch and a gentle peppery bite, lovely against the soft, sweet scallop and the citrus. It is served raw, so it stays crisp and cool.
new.kitchen: Cut it close to service: grated radish begins to lose its heat within the hour. How it is cut on the crudo, and which radish it is, are lineup questions.
new.compare: Horseradish shares the name and the mustard oil heat, but it is a different plant, a far stronger root grated as a condiment; a radish is mild enough to eat whole.

new.background: Where the radish was first grown is not settled: some botanists place it in the eastern Mediterranean, others in China or Southeast Asia, and it may have been domesticated more than once. Pliny the Elder (about 23 to 79) wrote that Egypt prized it for the oil pressed from its seed. Spanish missionaries brought radishes to Oaxaca in the sixteenth century, and there they became part of Christmas: since 1897 the city has held the Night of the Radishes on December 23, when growers carve outsized radishes into figures and scenes that last only a few hours before they wilt. Its bite is chemistry. A radish keeps glucosinolates and the enzyme myrosinase apart in its cells, and cutting or chewing lets them meet and form pungent isothiocyanates, the same family of compounds that gives mustard its heat.

deepen.background: The bay scallop, Argopecten irradians, lives in the eelgrass of shallow bays and sounds on the Atlantic coast and around the Gulf of Mexico, and it is short lived: it seldom lives two years, and in one study of New York's Peconic Bays fewer than one in a hundred harvested scallops had reached that age. From the 1870s to the mid 1980s its fishery from Massachusetts to North Carolina mattered both to the local economy and to the life of the towns that worked it. The scallop depends on its eelgrass, and when the eelgrass died off in the 1930s and again in the 1980s, scallop numbers and harvests fell hard. What reaches the plate is the adductor, the round muscle that closes the shell. Served on its own and raw, it is exempt under the FDA Food Code from the parasite freezing most raw fish needs.
deepen.metAt: Brennan's Thanksgiving Day 2026: Bay Scallop Crudo
deepen.guest: Our bay scallops are the small, sweet scallops of shallow bays, more tender than the larger sea scallops. On the crudo they are served raw, so you taste their natural sweetness, dressed with Meyer lemon, black truffle and radish.

deepen.background: The black truffle of the Périgord, Tuber melanosporum, is a winter truffle that grows underground on the roots of oaks and other trees in southern France, Spain and Italy; despite its name, most of the French crop comes from the south east. It is gathered from about November to March and found by scent, with trained dogs or pigs. Its cultivation began early in the nineteenth century in the Vaucluse, when a grower sowed acorns gathered under oaks that bore truffles and found truffles under the young trees, and in 1847 a grower at Carpentras planted oaks from such acorns over some seven hectares. A winter truffle of lesser aroma, Tuber brumale, grows in the same soils and is often confused with it. Jean Anthelme Brillat-Savarin (1755 to 1826) called the truffle the diamond of the art of cookery in The Physiology of Taste.
deepen.metAt: Brennan's Thanksgiving Day 2026: Bay Scallop Crudo
deepen.guest: Truffle is an underground fungus prized for its earthy, savory aroma. On the crudo it adds a deep, earthy note against the sweet raw scallops and the bright Meyer lemon; whether it is fresh or preserved, the kitchen can tell you.

deepen.background: Capers are the unopened flower buds of the caper bush, Capparis spinosa, a sprawling shrub that grows wild around the Mediterranean. The buds are picked by hand before they open and sorted by size with sieves or screens; the smaller the bud, the more it is valued, and nonpareil is the name of the smallest grade. Sorting is not exact, so one brand's nonpareils can run more even than another's. They are cured in salt or in brine, and salt packed capers are rinsed before use. On the volcanic island of Pantelleria, off Sicily, the Cappero di Pantelleria has carried the European Union's protected geographical indication since 1996. In French cooking, fish finished in brown butter with capers and lemon is served à la grenobloise, close kin to the meunière.
deepen.guest: Capers are the small flower buds of a Mediterranean shrub, picked before they open and cured in salt or brine. In the brown butter with the lemon they add a bright, briny pop that cuts through the richness of the redfish.
